title: A House for the Portrait
premise: Jude Pemberton takes a teaching job at Blackfen Primary to escape the grief and guilt of their grandmother's death, only to discover the school loses a child every few decades — and the old photographs from grandma's house have begun showing an extra chair that no one remembers. The chair belongs to Elsie Vane, a girl erased from the town's records in 1974, whose disappearance the school's founding families covered up and whose restless portrait hung in grandma's parlor all along. As Jude digs into what was taken — Elsie's name, her grave, her place in the town's memory — the house begins claiming rooms, then people, and Jude realizes the debt can only be paid by restoring Elsie to the record at the cost of their own family's name. In the end Jude burns the lie out of the town archive, seats Elsie in the portrait at last, and chooses to stay in Blackfen as its reluctant keeper of the truth, accepting that belonging sometimes means inheriting the thing everyone else fled.
about_author: Mara Hartwell is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who spent a decade collecting the small, wrong details of old houses before writing any of them down. They live in a converted parsonage with too many doors and insist, politely, that all of them are accounted for.

chapters.title: The Position at Blackfen
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Jude's POV. Jude arrives in the fading mill town of Blackfen to teach Year Six, renting the late grandmother's house on Vane Lane. The town feels politely watchful. Beat: uneasy new beginnings, grief disguised as a fresh start.

chapters.title: Twenty-Six Children
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The class register lists twenty-six names; only twenty-four desks fill. The headmaster, Corla Hesse, waves it off as a clerical error. Jude finds the same discrepancy in records going back decades. Beat: first crack in the town's surface.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Parlor
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, night. Unpacking grandma's belongings, Jude hangs the parlor portrait — a stern woman in a house interior with a single empty chair. That night, floorboards shift above like someone pacing. Jude tells themselves it's the boiler. Beat: denial established.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Sorting old family photographs, Jude notices every image from the house now includes an empty wooden chair that appears in none of their memories — including photos taken yesterday. Beat: the impossible made domestic; fear arrives quietly.

chapters.title: Roll Call
chapters.summary: Jude's POV at school. During attendance, a voice answers 'here' for a name Jude never read aloud. A girl in the back row — thin, grey-lipped — is gone when Jude looks up. The children don't react. Beat: the missing-class problem becomes personal.

chapters.title: Miss Hesse's Warning
chapters.summary: Dual focus, mostly Jude's POV with a short Corla section. Corla privately tells Jude some years the register 'runs long' and the correct response is to mark the child absent and move on. Her fear is older than her career. Beat: institutional complicity revealed.

chapters.title: Vane Lane After Dark
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The house rearranges at night: Jude's bedroom door opens onto the parlor, the portrait now facing the bed. The chair in the photographs has moved closer to the painted woman. Beat: the house is no longer passive.

chapters.title: The 1974 Yearbook
chapters.summary: Jude's POV at the county archive. A water-damaged 1974 school photo shows a girl half-scratched out; the caption reads 'Class of Mrs. Odell' with a name blotted by mold that won't wipe clean. Beat: the mystery acquires a date and a face.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. In grandma's locked sewing box: a child's shoe, a coroner's receipt, and a letter beginning 'I should have said something in '74.' The letter names the Vane family — and Jude's own grandfather. Beat: family guilt surfaces.

chapters.title: Elsie
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, dream sequence. Jude dreams of the parlor portrait from inside it: a girl, Elsie, sitting on the floor because the chair is 'not hers yet,' asking politely to be let back in. Jude wakes with floorboard grit in their palm. Beat: the ghost humanized.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Research reveals four surnames that still own half of Blackfen — Hesse, Odell, Crane, and Pemberton. In 1974 they collectively testified that Elsie Vane 'went to live with kin.' There was no kin. Beat: the conspiracy's shape emerges.

chapters.title: A Child Answers
chapters.summary: Jude's POV in class. Jude deliberately says the phantom name aloud; every pencil stops. The grey-lipped girl whispers 'you said it right' and the radiator runs cold. Corla witnesses the temperature drop. Beat: allies and witnesses begin to gather.

chapters.title: Corla's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Corla's POV. She recounts her own Year Six, 1987, when a boy named Tam answered roll for a year before 'the school let him rest' — after his mother publicly forgave the town at a council meeting. Truth spoken aloud, she implies, is the only currency the house accepts. Beat: rules of the haunting hinted.

chapters.title: The Chair in the Classroom
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. An empty wooden chair — identical to the one in the photographs — appears in Jude's classroom overnight. Children are drawn to sit in it; the girl who does speaks in a voice not her own. Jude removes the chair; it returns. Beat: escalation into the school itself.

chapters.title: Denholm Crane
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude approaches the eldest surviving founder, Denholm Crane, now in a care home. He mistakes Jude for his dead brother, confesses 'we voted her out of the world to save the school,' then lucidly warns Jude to stop. Beat: the crime confirmed by a perpetrator.

chapters.title: The House Takes a Room
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The parlor seals itself — wallpaper grown over the doorframe, the portrait now the only way to see inside. Jude hears grandma's voice among the trapped sounds, apologizing. Beat: grief weaponized; stakes become intimate.

chapters.title: The Missing File
chapters.summary: Jude's POV at the archive again. Elsie's records have been pulled; the archivist, a young Odell, is found weeping, unable to explain why she took them or where they are. The cover-up protects itself through people. Beat: the antagonist revealed as a system, not a villain.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: Corla's POV. Corla begs Jude to let it go — her own loyalty to Blackfen's children, she argues, requires the town stay stable enough to keep its school open. Jude realizes she believes this sincerely. Beat: theme of loyalty vs. truth given its strongest advocate.

chapters.title: The Second Chair
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. A second chair appears in the photographs — this one familiar: grandma's reading chair. The portrait now shows two empty seats and a door standing open in its painted background. Beat: the debt is widening; Jude's family is implicated as owed-thing, not just debtor.

chapters.title: Midnight Roll Call
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Woken at 3:14 a.m. — the timestamp on Elsie's coroner's receipt — Jude finds every photograph in the house turned face-down except the portrait, and hears a full class of children reciting names in the parlor. Beat: peak dread.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, assembling evidence. Elsie didn't vanish; she died in the school's care in 1974 — a fall down the parlor stairs of the building that became grandma's house — and the founders erased her to protect the school's funding charter. Beat: the full crime understood.

chapters.title: The Odell Girl
chapters.summary: The young archivist's POV. She returns the stolen file to Jude at night, shaking: 'It makes you take things. My family's been holding pieces for fifty years.' She gives up the file and her family's page of the testimony. Beat: the system cracks from within.

chapters.title: Retribution
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. That night the house takes something from Jude — twenty years of their own photographs now show Jude's chair empty, as if Jude had never sat anywhere. The house is practicing erasure on them. Beat: personal cost made visceral.

chapters.title: Corla's Confession, Part Two
chapters.summary: Corla's POV. She admits she was the child who answered roll for Tam in 1987, and that her silence since has been loyalty to the dead woman who taught her to keep the peace. She gives Jude the council meeting minutes from 1974. Beat: ally fully won; theme resolved in her arc.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Jude's POV at a tense town meeting Jude forces by reading Elsie's name into the public record. The founders' descendants react with fear, fury, and — in two cases — relief. The motion to restore Elsie's grave and name passes by one vote. Beat: justice begins outside the law, through witness.

chapters.title: The House Refuses
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The vote means nothing to the house: the chair remains empty, the parlor stays sealed, and the grey-lipped girl appears at Jude's classroom window at night. Words spoken in a chamber aren't the same as truth carried home. Beat: legal remedy insufficient; rising toward climax.

chapters.title: Carrying It Home
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude understands: the return must happen in the house, in the parlor, with the portrait as witness — and someone must speak every name the town took, including the founders' crimes, aloud, in full. Beat: the plan and its price clarified.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: Multi-POV vignettes. The Hesse, Odell, Crane, and Pemberton heirs each confront their inheritance; one burns his family papers, one flees town, Denholm Crane dies whispering Elsie's name. Beat: consequences radiating; the town's old order dissolving.

chapters.title: The Sealed Parlor
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude breaks into the sealed parlor through the portrait's painted door — physically, impossibly — and finds the room preserved as it was in 1974: dust, a fallen shoe, a child's coat on a hook. Beat: threshold crossed; no way back framed.

chapters.title: Every Name
chapters.summary: Jude's POV in the parlor. Jude begins the recitation: the erased children, the silenced teachers, the founders' lies. With each name, a chair in the painted room fills with a seated figure. The house shakes. Beat: the ritual of truth as the story's engine.

chapters.title: The Founders Interrupt
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The remaining descendants break in to stop the recitation, and in the struggle the portrait is nearly destroyed. The grey-lipped girl steps between them — visible to all now — and the room goes silent. Beat: climax's first collision.

chapters.title: Elsie's Testimony
chapters.summary: Elsie's POV, the only chapter in her voice. She tells what happened on the stairs in 1974, who carried her, who lied, who wept. The house holds everyone in the parlor until the account is heard entire. Beat: the victim reclaims the narrative; emotional core.

chapters.title: The Vote of the House
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The house itself renders judgment: the founders' portraits in the school corridor crack, their names flake from the plaque, and the charter funding dissolves into a trust in Elsie Vane's name. Beat: justice outside the law, enacted by the wronged.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair, Filled
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. In the final photograph — Jude takes it themselves — the parlor portrait shows Elsie seated in the chair, the painted woman's hand on her shoulder. The grey-lipped girl smiles once and is gone. Beat: the haunting's purpose fulfilled.

chapters.title: Aftermath: The Register
chapters.summary: Corla's POV. The new term's register lists twenty-seven names, all present, all accounted for. Corla reads every one aloud and marks each child 'here.' She weeps at her desk afterward. Beat: institutional redemption, small and earned.

chapters.title: What Jude Lost
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The house returns the parlor, the photographs, the memories — except grandma's voice, which stays with the house now. Jude grieves properly for the first time in twenty years. Beat: cost acknowledged; grief finally allowed.

chapters.title: The Question of Staying
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. With the mystery solved, Jude's contract ends and the outside world beckons. But the house has grown quiet in a way that feels like waiting, and the town's children need a teacher who knows the whole register. Beat: the belonging theme turned into a choice.

chapters.title: Keeper of the Record
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Jude accepts a new role — teacher, and unofficial archivist of the restored record — and moves fully into the house on Vane Lane, repainting the parlor but leaving one wall for the portrait. Beat: resolution of the loyalty question; Jude chooses truth as a way of life.

chapters.title: Open House
chapters.summary: Multi-POV. The town holds a memorial for Elsie; children lay flowers on her new headstone; Corla speaks; Denholm Crane's granddaughter apologizes publicly. The house on Vane Lane leaves its front door open all day. Beat: communal healing, earned and unsentimental.

chapters.title: The Chair by the Window
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, final chapter. Years later, a new teacher arrives in Blackfen and notices an extra chair in Jude's classroom. Jude smiles, says 'that one's spoken for,' and takes attendance — reading every name, and waiting, without fear, for every answer. Beat: cyclical ending; vigilance as inheritance; peace with a watchful edge.
